q: What is meant by the term ingestion?

pts.a: Taking in food (eating)

right: Ingestion is the taking in of food into the body.
wrong: The breakdown of food into small soluble molecules
The passage of digested food into the blood
The removal of undigested food from the body
why: Ingestion is taking food in through the mouth. It is the first step, followed by digestion, absorption and finally egestion.

q: What is meant by absorption in the digestive system?

pts.a: Digested food passing into the blood (or lymph)
accept: the passage of digested food into the bloodstream
soluble food moving into the lymph
food molecules taken into the blood

right: Absorption is the passage of digested food into the blood or lymph.
wrong: The taking in of food through the mouth
The breakdown of large food molecules into small ones
The removal of undigested food from the body
why: Absorption follows digestion: small soluble molecules pass through the gut wall, mostly in the villi of the ileum, into the blood or the lymph (lacteals).

q: Distinguish between ingestion and egestion.

pts.a: Ingestion: taking in food
accept: food is taken in through the mouth

pts.a: Egestion: removal of undigested food (faeces) from the body
accept: getting rid of faeces through the anus

right: Ingestion is taking in food; egestion is removing undigested food.
wrong: Ingestion is digesting food; egestion is removing urea from cells
Ingestion is taking in food; egestion is removing waste made by cells
Ingestion is absorbing food; egestion is breaking food down
why: Ingestion takes food in at the mouth. Egestion removes undigested food as faeces through the anus; removing waste made by cells is excretion.

q: State the function of the incisor teeth.

pts.a: Cutting (biting) food

right: Incisors cut and bite food.
wrong: They tear and grip meat
They grind and crush food
They mix food with saliva
why: Incisors are the flat, chisel-shaped teeth at the front. They cut and bite off pieces of food; canines tear, and premolars and molars grind.

q: State the function of the canine teeth.

pts.a: Tearing (gripping) food

right: Canines tear and grip food.
wrong: They cut and bite food
They grind and crush food
They push food to the back of the mouth
why: Canines are the pointed teeth beside the incisors. They tear and grip food; they are much longer in meat-eaters such as dogs.

q: State the function of the premolars and molars.

pts.a: Grinding (crushing) food

right: They grind and crush food.
wrong: They cut and bite food
They tear and grip food
They hold food while it is swallowed
why: Premolars and molars are the broad back teeth with cusps. They grind and crush food into small pieces, which gives enzymes a larger surface area.

q: Describe how the stomach breaks down food mechanically.

pts.a: Its muscular walls contract: churning
accept: the stomach wall churns the food
muscles in the wall contract and squeeze the food

pts.a: mixing the food with gastric juice into a liquid (chyme)
accept: mixes the food with acid and enzymes
makes it into a creamy liquid

right: Its muscular walls churn the food, mixing it with gastric juice.
wrong: Pepsin breaks proteins down into peptides
Hydrochloric acid kills the bacteria in the food
Bile emulsifies the fat into small droplets
why: Mechanical breakdown changes the size of the pieces, not the molecules: the stomach's muscle layers contract to churn the food, mixing it with gastric juice into a liquid called chyme.

q: Is churning in the stomach mechanical or chemical digestion? Explain your answer.

pts.a: Mechanical
It breaks food into smaller pieces without changing the molecules (no enzymes involved)
accept: it breaks food into small bits
the food is not changed chemically
it increases the surface area of the food

right: Mechanical: it breaks food into smaller pieces without using enzymes.
wrong: Chemical: pepsin breaks the protein into peptides
Chemical: the acid breaks the food into smaller pieces
Mechanical: enzymes break the large molecules into small ones
why: Churning only breaks food into smaller pieces and mixes it; no bonds are broken. Chemical digestion is done by enzymes such as pepsin, which break the molecules themselves.

q: Explain how churning in the stomach helps pepsin to digest protein.

pts.a: It mixes the food with gastric juice (pepsin), so the enzyme reaches all the food
accept: it mixes pepsin with the food
it breaks food into smaller pieces, giving a larger surface area for pepsin
it brings the enzyme into contact with the food

right: It mixes the food with gastric juice, so pepsin reaches all of it.
wrong: It makes the stomach alkaline, the pH pepsin needs
It absorbs the peptides into the blood
It adds bile, which emulsifies the protein
why: Churning mixes the food thoroughly with gastric juice, so pepsin and the acid reach every part of it, and the smaller pieces give the enzyme a larger surface area.

q: Name the enzyme that begins the digestion of starch in the mouth, and the product it forms.

pts.a: (Salivary) amylase
Maltose

right: Salivary amylase, which breaks starch down into maltose.
wrong: Pepsin, which breaks it down into peptides
Lipase, which breaks it down into fatty acids and glycerol
Salivary amylase, which breaks it down into amino acids
why: Saliva contains amylase, which works at about pH 7 and breaks starch into the sugar maltose. Pepsin acts on protein and lipase on fat.

q: Explain why salivary amylase stops working when food reaches the stomach.

pts.a: The stomach is acidic (about pH 2), which denatures amylase (its optimum is about pH 7)
accept: the pH is too low for it
it is denatured by the hydrochloric acid
the pH in the stomach is about 2

right: The stomach is too acidic, so the amylase is denatured.
wrong: There is no starch left by the time food reaches the stomach
The stomach is too cold for amylase to work
Bile from the liver breaks the amylase down
why: Amylase works best at about pH 7. The hydrochloric acid in the stomach gives about pH 2, which denatures it, so starch digestion only starts again in the duodenum.

q: Starch digestion is completed in the small intestine. Name the gland that makes the amylase that acts there, and the final product that is absorbed.

pts.a: Pancreas
Glucose

right: The pancreas; the final product absorbed is glucose.
wrong: The salivary glands; maltose is absorbed
The liver; glucose is absorbed
The pancreas; starch is absorbed whole
why: Pancreatic juice brings amylase into the duodenum to finish breaking starch into maltose, which is then broken into glucose, the sugar absorbed into the villi.

q: Food enters the duodenum at about pH 2, but the duodenum is about pH 8. Explain how the pH is raised.

pts.a: Bile and pancreatic juice are added
They are alkaline (contain sodium hydrogencarbonate), which neutralises the acid

right: Bile and pancreatic juice are alkaline, so they neutralise the acid.
wrong: The duodenum absorbs the hydrochloric acid into the blood
Pepsin uses up the acid as it digests protein
Bile adds more acid, which kills bacteria
why: Bile and pancreatic juice contain sodium hydrogencarbonate, an alkali that neutralises the stomach acid. This gives the pH of about 8 that lipase and pancreatic amylase need.

q: What is meant by deamination?

pts.a: Removal of the amino group from (excess) amino acids in the liver, forming urea
accept: breaking down spare amino acids to form urea
removing the nitrogen part of an amino acid
the amine group is removed from an amino acid
the NH2 group is removed from amino acids

right: Removing the amino group from spare amino acids, which forms urea.
wrong: Joining amino acids together to make proteins
Removing urea from the blood in the kidneys
Breaking down proteins into amino acids in the stomach
why: In the liver, the nitrogen-containing amino group is removed from amino acids the body does not need. It is turned into urea, which the kidneys excrete.

q: Describe what happens to excess amino acids in the liver.

pts.a: They are deaminated: the amino (nitrogen) group is removed
The amino group is converted into urea
The rest of the molecule is used for energy (respiration)
accept: the remainder is used to release energy

right: They are deaminated, forming urea, and the rest is used for energy.
wrong: They are stored in the liver until the body needs them
They are excreted unchanged in the urine
They are turned into urea and stored in the gall bladder
why: The body cannot store amino acids. The liver removes the amino group (deamination), which forms urea; the rest of the molecule is respired for energy.

q: Explain why the body deaminates excess amino acids.

pts.a: Amino acids (protein) cannot be stored in the body
accept: the body has no store for amino acids
the body is unable to store protein
the body does not store amino acids

right: Amino acids cannot be stored in the body, so spare ones are broken down.
wrong: So they can be stored as glycogen for later
So the liver can make bile from them
So the kidneys can turn them into urea
why: Unlike glucose (stored as glycogen) and fat, amino acids cannot be stored. Spare ones are deaminated in the liver: urea is formed and the rest is used for energy.

q: State what happens to absorbed glucose in the liver when the body does not need it straight away.

pts.a: It is converted to glycogen and stored

right: It is converted into glycogen and stored in the liver.
wrong: It is converted into glucagon and stored
It is converted into starch and stored
It is deaminated, forming urea
why: Glucose reaches the liver in the hepatic portal vein. The liver (and muscle) stores spare glucose as glycogen; starch is the store in plants, and glucagon is a hormone.

q: Explain why it is useful for the liver to store glucose as glycogen.

pts.a: Glucose can be released when needed (between meals), keeping the blood glucose level constant
accept: it keeps the blood sugar level steady
glycogen can be released as glucose when needed
it is a reserve of energy

right: Glucose can be released later, keeping the blood glucose level steady.
wrong: So the liver can turn the glucose into urea
So the glucose can be excreted in the urine
So the liver can use it to make bile
why: Between meals, glycogen is broken back down to glucose and released into the blood, so cells always have glucose for respiration and the blood glucose level stays steady.

q: Describe the route taken by a glucose molecule from the ileum to the liver.

pts.a: It is absorbed into the blood capillaries of a villus
accept: it passes into the capillaries in the villi
into the blood in the villi

pts.a: It is carried in the hepatic portal vein to the liver

right: Into the blood capillaries of the villi, then along the hepatic portal vein.
wrong: Into the lacteals of the villi, then along the lymph vessels
Into the capillaries of the villi, then along the hepatic artery
Into the lacteals, then along the hepatic vein
why: Glucose passes through the thin wall of a villus into its blood capillaries. These join the hepatic portal vein, which carries the food-rich blood straight to the liver.

q: Describe how faeces are formed in the large intestine.

pts.a: Water is absorbed from the undigested material (in the colon)
accept: water is reabsorbed into the blood
most of the water is taken back into the blood

pts.a: leaving undigested food (fibre), dead cells and bacteria
accept: what is left is mainly fibre and bacteria
the remaining undigested food, dead cells and bacteria

right: Water is absorbed, leaving undigested fibre, dead cells and bacteria.
wrong: Enzymes digest the remaining fat into fatty acids
Bile turns the leftover food solid
Water is added to the undigested food to soften it
why: As the undigested remains move through the colon, most of the water is absorbed into the blood. What is left (fibre, dead gut cells and bacteria) forms semi-solid faeces.

q: Name the part of the alimentary canal where faeces are stored before egestion.

pts.a: Rectum

right: In the rectum
wrong: In the appendix
In the anus
In the gall bladder
why: The rectum is the last part of the large intestine. It holds the faeces until they are egested through the anus.

q: Name the opening through which faeces leave the body.

pts.a: Anus

right: The anus
wrong: The rectum
The urethra
The colon
why: Faeces leave through the anus, at the end of the rectum: this is egestion. A ring of muscle keeps the anus closed until then. The urethra carries urine.

q: Explain why teenagers need more protein in their diet than elderly people.

pts.a: Teenagers are still growing: protein is needed to make new cells (tissue, muscle)
accept: they are growing and need to build new cells

right: Teenagers are still growing, and protein is needed to make new cells.
wrong: Protein is the main source of energy for teenagers
Protein is stored as fat to keep teenagers warm
Elderly people cannot digest protein at all
why: Protein gives the amino acids used to build new cells and tissues. Teenagers are growing fast, so they need more for their size; adults need it mainly for repair.

q: Explain why a very active person needs more carbohydrate in their diet than an inactive person.

pts.a: They use more energy, and carbohydrate (glucose) is the main source of energy for respiration
accept: more glucose is needed for respiration

right: They use more energy, and carbohydrate is the body's main energy source.
wrong: Carbohydrate builds and repairs their muscles
Carbohydrate replaces the salt lost in sweat
Carbohydrate makes their bones stronger
why: Muscles get their energy by respiring glucose. A very active person respires more, so needs more carbohydrate; an inactive person who eats too much stores the extra as fat.

q: Explain why teenage girls and women need more iron in their diet than men.

pts.a: To replace the blood (haemoglobin) lost in menstruation (periods)
accept: to replace blood lost in periods
they lose blood each month in menstruation
to make extra blood during pregnancy

right: Iron makes haemoglobin, and it replaces the blood lost during periods.
wrong: Iron is needed to build strong bones and teeth
Iron helps them to digest fat
Iron is needed to make the hormone oestrogen
why: Iron is part of haemoglobin in red blood cells. Females lose blood each month in menstruation (and make extra blood in pregnancy), so they need more iron to avoid anaemia.

q: Give two reasons why a balanced diet must include enough water.

pts.a: Water is the solvent (medium) for the chemical reactions in cells
accept: reactions in cells take place in water
most of the cytoplasm is water

pts.a: Transport of substances (blood plasma is mostly water)
accept: it carries food and wastes in the blood

pts.a: To replace the water lost in urine, sweat and breath (prevents dehydration)
accept: we lose water in urine and sweat every day

pts.a: Temperature control: sweating cools the body
Keeps the faeces soft, preventing constipation

right: It is the solvent for reactions in cells, and it replaces water lost in sweat.
wrong: It gives energy, and it builds and repairs muscle
It digests fat, and it makes the stomach acidic
It is stored as glycogen, and it makes bones hard
why: Most of a cell is water: its reactions take place dissolved in water, and blood plasma carries substances. Water is lost every day in urine, sweat and breath, so it must be replaced.

q: State one effect on health of a diet high in sugar.

pts.a: Obesity (weight gain), type 2 diabetes or tooth decay
accept: it can lead to type 2 diabetes

right: It can cause obesity and tooth decay.
wrong: It can cause scurvy
It can cause rickets
It can cause anaemia
why: Spare sugar is stored as fat, so a high-sugar diet can lead to obesity and type 2 diabetes, and mouth bacteria turn sugar into acid that decays teeth.

q: Explain how a diet high in sugar can cause tooth decay.

pts.a: Bacteria in the mouth (plaque) feed on the sugar
accept: micro-organisms in plaque feed on sugar

pts.a: They produce acid, which dissolves (attacks) the tooth enamel
accept: acid is made that dissolves the enamel
the acid wears away the enamel

right: Mouth bacteria feed on the sugar and make acid, which dissolves the enamel.
wrong: Sugar softens the enamel directly
Sugar stops calcium from reaching the teeth
Bacteria in the mouth turn the sugar into alcohol
why: Bacteria in plaque on the teeth respire the sugar and give off acid. The acid dissolves the hard enamel, making holes (cavities): tooth decay.

q: A vegan eats no food from animals. Name a nutrient that a vegan must take care to get enough of.

pts.a: Vitamin B12 (or iron, calcium, protein, iodine or vitamin D)

right: Vitamin B12, as it is found almost only in animal foods.
wrong: Vitamin C, found in fruit
Fibre, found in cereals
Carbohydrate, found in bread
why: Vitamin B12 comes almost only from animal foods, so vegans need fortified foods or supplements. Fibre, vitamin C and carbohydrate are easy to get from plants.

q: Name a plant food that is a good source of protein for a vegan.

pts.a: Beans, lentils, peas, nuts, seeds or soya (tofu)

right: Beans and lentils are rich in protein.
wrong: Cheese and yoghurt
Eggs
Apples and oranges
why: Vegans get protein from plants: pulses such as beans, lentils and peas, and nuts, seeds and soya (tofu). Cheese and eggs come from animals, and fruit has little protein.
